_“There has to be a ‘real reason’ and a ‘real justification’ which the Court would consider in order to invoke a Force Majeure clause”._ The Petitioner  relied upon  IMD data  reporting cumulative rainfall for the Nalanda district as a whole; the transmission asset was located specifically in Biharsharif, which is only one part of the district. Rainfall patterns can vary significantly within a district, and district-wide averages cannot be presumed to reflect the precise conditions at the specific project site. Even assuming but not admitting that there is any effect of such rainfall on the project site, the Petitioner is required to make efforts with due diligence and to mitigate the effect and had the Petitioner done so, the Petitioner could have achieved commercial operation in a timely. BSPHCL has submitted that under clause 14.4 of the Model TSA, timely notice of the force majeure event is a clear pre-condition to claim any relief. In the absence of any demonstrated compliance with this requirement, the entitlement to such relief is questionable. Therefore, the Petitioner’s claim for condonation of a 30-day time over-run on account of rainfall is liable to be rejected. Further, the Petitioner has not provided any reasoning for the cascading effect beyond 30 days.

31. The Petitioner, relying upon the case of Adyah Solar Energy Pvt. Ltd. v. KER and

Ors., has contended that the doctrine of _quantum meruit_ is applicable to the instant case. The Petitioner has contended that it would result in unjust enrichment if JSWEL and JPPL, who acquired the relevant assets/companies under the IBC processes, were permitted to retain the operational and commercial fruits of those assets without contribution in respect of transmission charges and relinquishment. We are unable to accept this contention of the Petitioner.  The principle of _quantum meruit_ , being an equitable doctrine, cannot be invoked to circumvent the statutory scheme of the IBC or to revive claims which have attained finality under the IBC. In the present case, the Petitioner's claims towards transmission charges and relinquishment charges were admittedly lodged before the Resolution Professional/ Liquidator pursuant to the directions of this Commission and were thereafter dealt with in the insolvency/liquidation proceedings. The rights and liabilities of the stakeholders consequently came to be governed by the approved Resolution Plan in terms of Section 31 of the IBC and the waterfall mechanism under Section 53 of the IBC. We are of the view that once the claims have been subjected to the statutory framework of the IBC and the proceedings have attained finality, the equitable doctrine of _quantum meruit_ cannot be invoked to confer upon the Petitioner a right of recovery beyond what is permissible under the IBC.

To the extent the Petitioner was aggrieved by the treatment of its claims in the insolvency or liquidation proceedings, or by the orders passed by NCLT, the remedy, if any, lay under the provisions of the IBC. The present proceedings cannot be invoked as an indirect means of obtaining relief inconsistent with, or beyond the statutory framework governing insolvency and liquidation. This Commission cannot, in exercise of its regulatory jurisdiction, revisit or modify the orders passed under the IBC.

45. In view of the foregoing discussion, we are of the considered view that the Petitioner's claims have already been dealt with in accordance with the provisions of the IBC and the legal consequences flowing therefrom have attained finality. Neither the Act nor any of the Regulations confer any power upon this Commission to direct recovery of the unrecovered transmission charges and relinquishment charges in matters which have already been decided under the IBC 2016.
